beats.text: First, authentication. The job authenticates with the GITHUB_TOKEN, the short-lived token every job gets, and needs packages: write. beats.text: Second, how tags and content are produced. The metadata action derives tags and labels from the Git ref and commit. The build action builds and, with push: true, pushes. beats.text: Third, and this is the sentence of the video: an image is identified by its digest, not by a tag. The digest is a fingerprint computed from the image's content. Whether a working tree is exactly a commit: git status in its short or porcelain form prints nothing when it is. And what that commit is called relative to the release tags: git describe with --tags and --match for the release pattern.

beats.text: Releases, in outline. Three facts and one trap.
beats.tele: Releases, in outline. Three facts and one trap.

beats.text: Fact one. A release is a GitHub object on a Git tag. In a job, gh release create with the tag, the files, --verify-tag and --generate-notes creates it, with the token in the environment and contents: write permission. --verify-tag refuses to invent a tag that doesn't exist. You saw why that matters in video 140: without it the command may create a tag on the default branch, and section 15.22 labels that form 🔴 DANGEROUS. With --verify-tag and --draft the label is 🟡 CAUTION.
beats.tele: Fact one. A release is a GitHub object on a Git tag. In a job, `gh release create` with the tag, the files, `--verify-tag` and `--generate-notes` creates it, with the token in the environment and `contents: write` permission. `--verify-tag` refuses to invent a tag that doesn't exist. You saw why that matters in video 140: without it the command may create a tag on the default branch, and section 15.22 labels that form 🔴 DANGEROUS. With `--verify-tag` and `--draft` the label is 🟡 CAUTION.

beats.text: Fact two. With immutable releases, create a draft, attach every asset, then publish.
beats.tele: Fact two. With immutable releases, create a draft, attach every asset, then publish.

beats.text: Fact three. Tools such as release-please derive the release from conventional commit messages. The textbook is explicit: it's named as a concept and wasn't run for the book.

beats.text: Quick quiz. One workflow creates a release with the job token. A second workflow has the trigger on: release. Does the second one start? A, yes. B, no. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. One workflow creates a release with the job token. A second workflow has the trigger `on: release`. Does the second one start? A, yes. B, no. Your answer?

beats.text: The trap. B, it doesn't. Events caused by the GITHUB_TOKEN don't start new workflow runs, with narrow exceptions. A workflow that creates a tag or a release with the job token won't trigger your separate on: release or tag-push workflow.
beats.tele: The trap. B, it doesn't. Events caused by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` don't start new workflow runs, with narrow exceptions. A workflow that creates a tag or a release with the job token won't trigger your separate `on: release` or tag-push workflow.

beats.text: The textbook gives two ways out. Either chain the work as jobs of one workflow with needs. Or create the tag with a GitHub App token.
beats.tele: The textbook gives two ways out. Either chain the work as jobs of one workflow with `needs`. Or create the tag with a GitHub App token.

beats.text: Why does GitHub do this? You heard the rule in video 143 as a property of the job token. Think about the alternative: a workflow that pushes with its own token and thereby starts itself again.

beats.text: There are three kinds of names on an image, and each has a twin in Git.

beats.text: A tag like main or latest behaves like a branch: it's a name that moves when someone pushes.
beats.tele: A tag like `main` or `latest` behaves like a branch: it's a name that moves when someone pushes.

beats.text: A tag like 0.2.0 behaves like a release tag: it's meant to stay, and nothing but discipline makes it stay.
beats.tele: A tag like `0.2.0` behaves like a release tag: it's meant to stay, and nothing but discipline makes it stay.

beats.text: The model you built in Part 1, that a branch is a ref and a commit ID is the identity, carries over directly. Deploying :latest is like deploying "whatever main is at the moment the machine pulls".

beats.text: Where the comparison breaks: a commit ID covers the source. A digest covers the built image. You record both, together, and that pair is what answers the on-call engineer's question.

beats.text: git restore on a path is 🔴 DANGEROUS, so the five answers before it runs. What it changes: the file in the working tree, from the index. What it can destroy: uncommitted edits to that file that were never staged. How to preview: git diff for the path. How to recover: there is no recovery for content that was never staged. When it's appropriate: here, for a one-line tweak made on purpose in a sandbox, after git status showed that it's the only change.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Deploying by a tag such as latest or main. Root cause: a tag is a movable name, exactly like a branch; only the digest identifies the image.
beats.tele: Deploying by a tag such as `latest` or `main`. Root cause: a tag is a movable name, exactly like a branch; only the digest identifies the image.

beats.text: Building a release image on a laptop. Root cause: the working tree may differ from the commit it claims to be; a runner's checkout is clean.
beats.tele: Building a release image on a laptop. Root cause: the working tree may differ from the commit it claims to be; a runner's checkout is clean.

beats.text: A release workflow that waits for an event its own token caused. Root cause: events caused by the GITHUB_TOKEN do not start new workflow runs, with narrow exceptions.
beats.tele: A release workflow that waits for an event its own token caused. Root cause: events caused by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not start new workflow runs, with narrow exceptions.

beats.text: Deriving the version from a tag in a job with the default checkout. Root cause: one commit and no tags, so git describe has nothing to find.
beats.tele: Deriving the version from a tag in a job with the default checkout. Root cause: one commit and no tags, so `git describe` has nothing to find.

beats.text: Omitting context: . after steps that changed files. Root cause: by default the build action builds from the Git context and ignores local file changes.
beats.tele: Omitting `context: .` after steps that changed files. Root cause: by default the build action builds from the Git context and ignores local file changes.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A team that serves a ranking model has two workflows. The first runs on pushes to main: it tests, computes the next version, and creates a release with the job token. The second has the trigger on: release and builds and publishes the image. The first workflow goes green. A release appears. The second workflow never starts, and for a day people look for a typing error in its trigger.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. A team that serves a ranking model has two workflows. The first workflow goes green. A release appears. The second workflow never starts, and for a day people look for a typing error in its trigger.

beats.text: There is none. The release was created by the GITHUB_TOKEN, and events caused by that token don't start new workflow runs.
